title: Behavioral economics & consumer psychology principles for UX/Product

darkPatternScale.3: Pressure - pushes quick or bigger decisions
darkPatternScale.4: Manipulative - works against the user's interest

darkPatternNote: Ratings judge the dark pattern example, not the principle itself.

principles.name: Anchoring
principles.description: The first number or option people see becomes a reference point that skews how they judge everything after it.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows a serum at $49 next to a crossed-out $85 it was never sold for.
principles.darkPatternReason: A fake price is misleading, and degrades trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store only shows a crossed-out $85 if the serum was really sold at that price recently.

principles.name: Decoy Effect
principles.description: Adding a clearly inferior option makes a nearby target option look better by comparison.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store adds a $32 medium moisturizer that only exists to make the $34 large look like a steal.
principles.darkPatternReason: A fake option steers shoppers, and feels sneaky once noticed.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers small, medium and large sizes that each suit a real need.

principles.name: Charm Pricing
principles.description: Prices ending in .99 or .95 are perceived as noticeably lower because people anchor on the left-most digit.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store prices a lipstick at $19.99 so it feels closer to $19 than $20.
principles.darkPatternReason: It's a mild trick that most shoppers accept.
principles.healthyExample: The store uses $19.99 pricing but shows the full total clearly at checkout.

principles.name: Price Relativity
principles.description: People judge value relative to what's around it, not in absolute terms.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store places a $45 foundation next to a $120 one so the $45 feels cheap.
principles.darkPatternReason: It nudges spending, but nothing is hidden.
principles.healthyExample: The store compares foundations side by side by size and ingredients, not just price.

principles.name: Mental Accounting
principles.description: People put money into separate mental 'pots' (gifts, treats, essentials) and spend differently from each.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store labels a $30 face mask a 'self-care treat' to make it feel guilt-free.
principles.darkPatternReason: It softens spending, which can lead to buyer's regret.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers an 'Under $15' section to help shoppers stick to a budget.

principles.name: Pain of Paying
principles.description: Paying feels like a loss; the more visible and immediate the payment, the more it hurts.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store pushes 'Pay in 4' on every product page so a $90 bundle feels cheap.
principles.darkPatternReason: Hiding the real cost encourages debt, and causes regret later.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows the full $90 total and payment schedule before shoppers choose 'Pay in 4'.

principles.name: Zero-Price Effect
principles.description: 'Free' has a disproportionate pull, far stronger than a small price reduction.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store offers free shipping over $35, so a shopper adds a $6 lip balm they don't need.
principles.darkPatternReason: It nudges a bigger basket, but the deal is clear.
principles.healthyExample: The store suggests refills of products the shopper already uses to reach free shipping.

principles.name: Partitioned Pricing
principles.description: Splitting a price into parts (or revealing fees late) makes the total feel lower. Often seen as a dark pattern.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store adds a $4.50 delivery fee and a $1 packaging fee on the last checkout step.
principles.darkPatternReason: Hidden fees deceive shoppers, and destroy trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows the full price, including delivery, on the product page.

principles.name: Choice Overload
principles.description: Too many options increase decision time and can lead to no decision at all.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows all 140 foundation shades on one huge page.
principles.darkPatternReason: Too many options overwhelm shoppers, so they leave without buying.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers a 3-question quiz that narrows the shades down to 4 matches.

principles.name: Default Effect
principles.description: People tend to stick with whatever option is pre-selected.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store pre-selects a $25 monthly subscription at checkout.
principles.darkPatternReason: Shoppers get charged without meaning to, and feel tricked.
principles.healthyExample: The store defaults to a one-off purchase and offers the subscription as a clear opt-in.

principles.name: Framing Effect
principles.description: The same information leads to different decisions depending on how it's presented.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store says '97% saw fewer breakouts' but hides that only 30 people were tested.
principles.darkPatternReason: Selective facts mislead shoppers, and erode trust when found out.
principles.healthyExample: The store says '97% saw fewer breakouts' and links to the full study.

principles.name: Compromise Effect
principles.description: When given three options, people tend to choose the middle one to avoid extremes.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store makes the $35 gift set the obvious pick, even though the $15 set suits most shoppers.
principles.darkPatternReason: Steering people away from what suits them erodes trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store explains who each gift set is for, so shoppers pick the right one.

principles.name: Choice Architecture
principles.description: The way choices are laid out shapes which one people pick, without removing any options.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store hides the cheapest shipping option below the fold at checkout.
principles.darkPatternReason: Burying options costs shoppers money, and feels unfair.
principles.healthyExample: The store lists every shipping option clearly, with the eco option highlighted.

principles.name: Cognitive Load
principles.description: People have limited mental capacity; extra effort or information reduces completion and good decisions.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store makes canceling a subscription a confusing 6-step process.
principles.darkPatternReason: Deliberate friction traps shoppers, and breeds resentment.
principles.healthyExample: The store lets shoppers cancel a subscription in one click.

principles.name: Satisficing
principles.description: Most people pick the first option that's 'good enough' rather than searching for the best.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store puts a 'Best for dry skin' badge on its highest-profit moisturizer.
principles.darkPatternReason: A biased badge misleads shoppers, and damages credibility.
principles.healthyExample: The store awards 'Best for dry skin' badges based on reviews and ingredients.

principles.name: Loss Aversion
principles.description: Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store emails 'Don't lose your $5 credit!' two days before it expires.
principles.darkPatternReason: Fear of loss rushes shoppers, and can feel pushy.
principles.healthyExample: The store reminds shoppers about their $5 credit a week before it expires.

principles.name: Endowment Effect
principles.description: People value things more once they feel they own them.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store sends a free trial serum, then charges $60 if it isn't returned within 7 days.
principles.darkPatternReason: Surprise charges make shoppers feel tricked.
principles.healthyExample: The store sends a free sample with no strings attached.

principles.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
principles.description: People continue investing in something because of what they've already put in.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store tells shoppers they're 80 points from a reward, then raises the target.
principles.darkPatternReason: Moving the goalposts exploits effort already spent, and breaks trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store keeps reward targets fixed, and points never expire.

principles.name: Risk Aversion
principles.description: People avoid choices with unclear outcomes; reducing uncertainty increases action.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store advertises free returns but charges a $7 restocking fee on opened items.
principles.darkPatternReason: Hidden conditions mislead shoppers, and damage trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers free returns, even on opened products.

principles.name: Zero-Risk Bias
principles.description: People prefer eliminating a small risk completely over reducing a larger risk partially.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store sells $8 'breakage protection' that the courier already covers for free.
principles.darkPatternReason: Selling fake peace of mind wastes money, and erodes trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers a simple money-back guarantee with no conditions.

principles.name: Social Proof
principles.description: People copy what others are doing, especially under uncertainty.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows '2,341 bought this week' when the number is made up.
principles.darkPatternReason: Fake numbers deceive shoppers, and destroy credibility.
principles.healthyExample: The store only shows real purchase numbers from the last 7 days.

principles.name: Authority Bias
principles.description: People trust and follow perceived experts or credible institutions.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store adds a 'Dermatologist recommended' badge with no named expert behind it.
principles.darkPatternReason: An unbacked claim misleads shoppers, and damages credibility.
principles.healthyExample: The store names the dermatologist behind the 'recommended' badge.

principles.name: Liking / Similarity
principles.description: People are more persuaded by those they like or who seem similar to them.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows paid influencer reviews styled to look like regular customers.
principles.darkPatternReason: Disguised ads deceive shoppers, and destroy trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store lets shoppers filter reviews by 'skin like mine' and labels paid reviews.

principles.name: Reciprocity
principles.description: When given something, people feel obliged to give something back.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store adds a free mini lip oil, then sends daily emails pushing the $28 full size.
principles.darkPatternReason: Turning a gift into pressure feels pushy, and annoys shoppers.
principles.healthyExample: The store adds a free mini lip oil as a thank-you, with no sales follow-up.

principles.name: Commitment
principles.description: Once people make a small commitment, they're more likely to follow through with bigger, consistent actions.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store makes shoppers enter their email to see their skin quiz results.
principles.darkPatternReason: Gating results feels like a bait and switch.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows skin quiz results right away, with no sign-up needed.

principles.name: Scarcity Effect
principles.description: Things seem more valuable when they appear limited.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows 'Only 3 left!' on every product, all the time.
principles.darkPatternReason: Fake scarcity deceives shoppers, and destroys trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store only shows stock levels when they're real.

principles.name: Urgency
principles.description: Time limits push people to act sooner rather than defer.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows a sale countdown that resets every time the page reloads.
principles.darkPatternReason: A fake deadline deceives shoppers, and breaks trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store only uses countdowns for real sales that end when stated.

principles.name: Exclusivity
principles.description: Access that feels restricted to a select group increases desire.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store hides its best prices behind a $9.99 monthly membership.
principles.darkPatternReason: Locking deals behind a fee feels exclusionary, and pushes spending.
principles.healthyExample: The store gives members early access to new launches, with the same prices for everyone.

principles.name: Goal-Gradient Effect
principles.description: People speed up as they get closer to a goal.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store's free shipping bar says '$4 to go' but only suggests $20 products.
principles.darkPatternReason: It pushes shoppers to overspend, and feels manipulative.
principles.healthyExample: The store's free shipping bar suggests small, useful items like refills.

principles.name: Endowed Progress Effect
principles.description: Giving people artificial head-start progress makes them more likely to complete a goal.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store gives 2 free loyalty stamps, then quietly makes stamps expire after 30 days.
principles.darkPatternReason: Hidden expiry rules frustrate shoppers, and erode loyalty.
principles.healthyExample: The store gives 2 free loyalty stamps that never expire.

principles.name: Variable Rewards
principles.description: Unpredictable rewards are more motivating and habit-forming than predictable ones.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows a 'spin to win' wheel after every purchase.
principles.darkPatternReason: Gambling-style rewards build compulsive habits.
principles.healthyExample: The store gives a free sample of the shopper's choice with every 5th order.

principles.name: Hyperbolic Discounting
principles.description: People prefer smaller rewards now over bigger rewards later.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store offers 15% off today only if shoppers open a store credit card.
principles.darkPatternReason: A quick reward hides a long-term cost, and can lead to debt.
principles.healthyExample: The store offers 15% off a first order with no strings attached.

principles.name: Zeigarnik Effect
principles.description: People remember and feel pulled to finish incomplete tasks.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store nags 'Your profile is 60% complete' until shoppers share their phone number.
principles.darkPatternReason: Pressuring for personal data feels intrusive, and erodes trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store explains why each profile detail helps, and makes every field optional.

principles.name: IKEA Effect
principles.description: People value things more when they've helped create them.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store lets shoppers build a custom gift box, then adds a $5 'assembly fee' at checkout.
principles.darkPatternReason: A surprise fee exploits the effort shoppers put in, and feels unfair.
principles.healthyExample: The store lets shoppers build a custom gift box with a running total on screen.

principles.name: Peak-End Rule
principles.description: People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and how it ended.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store ends every order with a delightful animation, but makes returns a hassle.
principles.darkPatternReason: A nice ending masks a poor experience that shoppers remember later.
principles.healthyExample: The store ends each order with a friendly thank-you and clear tracking info.

principles.name: Serial Position Effect
principles.description: People remember the first and last items in a list best.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store always puts its highest-profit products first and last in search results.
principles.darkPatternReason: It quietly steers shoppers, and can hide better options.
principles.healthyExample: The store orders search results by relevance and labels sponsored items.

principles.name: Von Restorff Effect
principles.description: The item that stands out visually is the one most likely to be noticed and remembered.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store labels its $40 premium plan 'Most popular' when it isn't.
principles.darkPatternReason: A false label misleads shoppers, and damages trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store highlights the plan that's genuinely best for most shoppers.

principles.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
principles.description: People assume attractive designs work better and attribute positive traits based on one good impression.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store uses heavily retouched before-and-after photos for a wrinkle cream.
principles.darkPatternReason: Fake results mislead shoppers, and lead to disappointment.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows unretouched photos from real customers.

principles.name: Mere Exposure Effect
principles.description: The more people see something, the more they tend to like it.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store follows shoppers around the web with ads for a product they viewed once.
principles.darkPatternReason: Constant tracking feels creepy, and erodes trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows recently viewed items only on its own site.

principles.name: Priming
principles.description: Exposure to one stimulus unconsciously influences response to the next.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store shows spa-style images and 'You deserve this' copy before $120 night creams.
principles.darkPatternReason: It sets a spending mood, but nothing is hidden.
principles.healthyExample: The store pairs calming images with clear prices and ingredients.

principles.name: Confirmation Bias
principles.description: People seek and favor information that supports what they already believe.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store labels products 'toxin-free' to match what clean beauty shoppers already believe.
principles.darkPatternReason: Vague claims exploit beliefs, and spread misinformation.
principles.healthyExample: The store explains what its 'clean' label actually means.

principles.name: Ambiguity Effect
principles.description: People avoid options where key information is missing.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store leaves the ingredient list off its bestselling serum.
principles.darkPatternReason: Missing info stops informed choices, and erodes trust.
principles.healthyExample: The store shows the full ingredient list on every product.

principles.name: Labor Illusion
principles.description: People value results more when they can see the effort behind them.
principles.darkPatternExample: The store adds a fake 5-second 'Analyzing your skin...' delay before quiz results.
principles.darkPatternReason: Faking effort is misleading, and feels cheap when noticed.
principles.healthyExample: The store only shows progress messages while the tool is actually working.
